units: the writer sends news to a close acquaintance about a plot of ground taken back in hand
a layer of plant matter has been spread over the soil to hold the moisture
the hedge has been filled out with cuttings taken from shrubs
the plants chosen can stand a shortage of water
building rubble has to be hauled away because it blocks water from soaking in
the writer notices that rain is held better since the work was done
the roots reach farther down than they used to
the writer asks after the food garden of the person written to
text: Dear friend, I finally have something to tell you about the plot we took back in hand behind the house. Three jobs have kept me busy, and here they are in turn. The ground came first. I spread a thick blanket of dead leaves over it, which holds the damp in and slows the drying out. The hedge came second. I filled its gaps with cuttings pulled off the shrubs that shrug off a dry spell. The third job is the dreary one, hauling away the rubble the old shed left behind, since it keeps water from soaking in. Already the leaf layer drinks up the rain better, and the roots are reaching farther down than they used to. If the weather keeps swinging the way people warn it will, these small chores will beat regret. Write back soon, and tell me how your vegetable patch is coming along.

units: a heavy fuel escaped from a storage yard into a watercourse
the leak went unnoticed through the first week
fishermen then saw fish that had gone weak
a colored film spread across the surface of the water
the technical services moved only once the drinking supply was threatened
floating devices were put in place to hold back the slick
the fouled sediment was scraped off after the pumping
wildlife is coming back to the site little by little
a smell lingers on the bank when the heat builds
text: So you want to know what has gone on in the river since the trouble at the fuel storage yard? Here it is, in order. Through that whole first week nobody caught on at all. The heavy oil was seeping out under a cracked slab, and from the bank there was nothing to smell and nothing to see. Then the anglers began pulling up listless fish, and a rainbow film crept out across the flat water. Did anyone move fast, you ask? Honestly, no. The crews turned out only once the slick had reached the drinking water intake. After that it all went quickly. Floating booms went in, the oily layer was pumped off, and the fouled silt underneath was scraped away. And now? Now the wildlife is drifting back, slowly, though the bank still gives off a tarry smell whenever the heat builds. That is where things stand.

units: the spring that feeds an upper district is running dry
the water drawn for crops has emptied the underground table
a grower fears losing his harvest without irrigation
a schoolteacher asks the manager about supply brought in by truck
the manager admits that this would become necessary the following summer
the council intends to cap the volumes it allows
the leaking pipes will be repaired
the watering of ornamental ground will be forbidden
those present admit that their own habits add to the shortage
text: The woman who runs the water service put it plainly to the residents gathered in the lower hall. The spring that feeds the upper district is running dry. Farm pumping had emptied the table underground through the dry months, she said, and one thing was dragging the next along behind it. A grower shot back that without irrigation his crops would burn. A schoolteacher asked whether the children would end up drinking water trucked in from somewhere else. That, the manager admitted, was what the following summer would bring unless something changed. The council would cap the volumes it allowed, patch the leaking mains, and forbid the watering of lawns. The meeting ran late, and by the end everyone could see that the shortage came not from the sky alone but from what every household drew.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the channel of a harbor was filling with deposits season after season
ships could no longer work their way up to the quays
the merchants believed wrongly that the sea was pulling away
the river was in fact carrying down sediment torn off the slopes
the felling of trees had left the hillsides with no cover
engineers tied the ruin of the heights to the decline of the harbor
plantings were ordered along the ridges
works of woven brushwood were set into the gullies
basins were dug to trap the mud before the shore
the depth of the navigable passage was won back
text: A thriving harbor town once watched its channel fill in, season after season. Ships loaded with salt and timber scraped bottom, then gave up on reaching the quays. The merchants worried, sure the sea was pulling away from them, when in truth the river kept carrying down into the roads a load of silt torn off the slopes above. Timber felled for roof beams had left those slopes with nothing on them, and rain now cut the soil with nothing to slow it. A generation of engineers finally tied the skinned hillside to the failing harbor. They had the ridges replanted, brushwood woven along the gullies, and basins dug where the mud could settle before it ever reached the shore. The channel won back its depth, and the lesson outlived those who learned it. No one heals a shore without tending the heights above it.

units: two roofs sharing a wall behave in different ways under the sun
the first carries a dark bituminous covering
that surface takes in nearly all the sunlight that reaches it
the heating damages the insulation laid beneath
the cooling equipment then runs without a break
the second pairs a pale coating with a cover of plants
that roof throws back part of the sunlight and stores rainwater
the pale one stays cooler when both are read at the same hour
the planted roof weighs more and calls for steady upkeep
text: Two roofs share a wall and answer the sun in opposite ways, and the covering is what explains it. The first wears a dark bituminous membrane, close to tar, which soaks up almost every bit of sunlight that lands on it. The surface climbs so hot that the insulation laid beneath it ages early and the cooling equipment never shuts off. The second carries a pale mineral coating topped with a mat of thick-leaved plants. It throws back a good share of the sunlight and keeps rainwater in its growing bed. Read at the same hour, the pale roof stays markedly cooler than the dark one. The gap turns up on the energy bill of the building as well. On the other hand, a planted roof weighs more and asks for steady upkeep, which the membrane never does. So the choice rests on the framing as much as on the weather.

units: the keeper of a high mountain station tells of a stretch of his last measuring season
the packed snow was covered with a grayish deposit
that deposit had come from fires burning far away
a darkened surface takes in more heat and melts faster
the buried instruments had to be dug out twice in the same week
the slope was strangely quiet at night
the usual nighttime trickle of water had gone
the observer wrote down what he saw in a notebook
the readings of the seasons that followed bore out his impression
text: The keeper of a high mountain station tells of one stretch of his last measuring season that he has never shaken off. He starts with the color of the old packed snow. Instead of the white he expected, a gray veil of soot lay across the whole of it, carried in from fires burning far away. He goes on to the melt, which ran fast, because darkened snow takes in more heat than clean snow does. He describes the buried sensors too, dug out twice in a single week as the pack sank under them. Last he brings up the quiet, a slope stripped of the night trickle of meltwater that used to keep him company. Back at the shelter he wrote it all into a bound logbook, aware that one man's story proves nothing. The readings of the seasons that followed bore him out, and his notebook seeded a far wider study.

units: the roof must be looked over and clean before any water is collected
a screen goes into the mouth of the gutter to hold back leaves
the tank is set on firm footing and out of the sun
a collector fitted with a filter joins the downspout to the tank
the overflow must run off toward planted ground and not toward the street
the water of the first week serves to rinse and is then thrown out
the seal of the lid is checked every season
an open container helps mosquitoes breed
the store is drawn down partway before the frost to keep the wall from splitting
text: Before you start collecting rainwater at home, look the roof over. A clean covering, free of moss and grime, will give you clearer water. Next, drop a strainer into the mouth of the gutter so that the leaves stay out. Set the tank on firm footing and well out of the sun, since warmth feeds algae. Join the downspout to it with a collector that carries a filter, and make sure the overflow can run off into a planted bed rather than onto the street. Open the tap through the whole of the first week to rinse the tank, then throw that water out. Every season, check that the lid still seals, because an open container breeds mosquitoes. Last of all, draw the store down partway before the frost sets in, or the ice will split the wall. Water of this kind suits the garden and the washing of tools.

units: an old shore path has been closed off with a fence
the sea is hollowing out the foot of the rock wall
storms have come around more often
each swell carries off soft rock at the base of the bank
the upper part ends up giving way
a house was pulled down over the cold season before
its rubble still litters the beach below
an official explains that pulling back and holding on both come dear
researchers find the pace quickening as the water rises
the parking areas are being shifted inland
text: What hits you first up on the cliff is the orange mesh strung across the old shore path. The people who live here will tell you straight off that the sea is eating the foot of the wall and the top follows. Storms come around more often now, and every heavy swell tears another bite of soft rock out of the base, until the harder stuff overhead tips forward. One house had to be pulled down over the cold season before, and its rubble still litters the beach below. The official in charge of the shore makes no secret of his bind. Pulling back comes dear, and holding on comes dearer. The researchers who came to measure the retreat find the pace quickening as the water rises. For now the parking areas get shifted, access gets closed off, warnings get posted. And each winter the fence moves farther inland.

units: a wet meadow looks from a distance like an ordinary field
straight ditches were cut long ago to drain the marsh
that draining was meant to win grazing ground
the water runs off toward a canal instead of sitting in the hollows
the peat laid open to the air gives up its carbon
the birds that nested in the rushes have left the place
a crew of managers stops the ditches with clay
the water table is lifted and the reeds come back
walkways keep visitors away from the tender ground
frogs and newts moved into the pools by the second season
text: Seen from the towpath, the wet meadow could pass for an ordinary field, grassy and cropped short. Walk closer and the straight ditches show up, cut long ago to dry the marsh out and win grazing ground for livestock. The water now slides off toward the canal instead of sitting in the hollows, and the peat, laid open to the air, breaks down and gives up its carbon. The birds that nested in the rush clumps have gone. A crew of managers is working to tip the balance back. They stop the ditches with clay plugs, lift the water table and let the reeds crowd in again. Wooden walkways steer walkers away from the tender ground. By the second season the refilled pools had taken in frogs and newts, and the soaked peat had stopped smoldering. The ground looks messier, and that is the sign they were waiting for.

units: the writer disputes the sporting image used to describe work on the climate
a race is run alone and closes at a set finish
the writer offers instead the image of ground worked in common
each person there takes over the soil the others left behind
whoever neglects a patch in a garden harms the plot alongside
changing the image changes the kind of commitment expected
a promise with a figure on it differs from a promise of steady upkeep
the writer calls for talk of care rather than of performance
the generations to come will judge what has lasted
text: We like to talk about work on the climate as a race, with winners out front and stragglers behind. The picture is appealing, and it misleads. A race is run alone and it closes. Climate sits closer to a shared garden, where each of us takes over the soil the last hands left behind. Slow down in a race and you lose your place. Let your patch go in a garden and the weeds walk straight into the bed alongside. That difference is no decoration. It changes what we ought to expect from the commitments people make. A runner promises a score. A gardener promises to keep showing up. One measures an arrival, the other a continuity. We would do better, then, to speak less of records and more of care, less of standings and more of seasons. Those who come after us will not ask who ran hardest. They will look at what is still growing.
